newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK people flock to snap last traces of colonial rule.
newsitem.headline: HK people flock to snap last traces of colonial rule.

text.p: Hong Kong people queued outside Government House on Sunday armed with cameras and video recorders to take a final snapshot of British colonial power in the territory.

Large crowds had gathered in bright sunshine and shot off reels of film of the Union Jack flags hanging from poles outside Governor Chris Patten's residence and the nearby Central Government Office which bears the colonial power's coat of arms.
Later the crowds became so dense that they had to organise a queue and wait their turn to take souvenir pictures
Hong Kong reverts to Beijing control at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday after 156 years of colonial rule.

"We are here to take pictures before the crown disappears," said Lee Chun-ming as he took photos of his wife and two sons outside the side gate of the stately mansion on the slopes of Hong Kong Island.
"We want the kids to know about it in the future. They are too young now," said Lee, who travelled from his home in the industrial suburb of Tsuen Wan.
Asked how he felt about the imminent handover, Lee, with a camera on one shoulder and a video camera on the other, said he was a little apprehensive.
"If things can stay the same then it would be all right."
One local resident, who gave his last name as Pang and who came with his wife and daughter, echoed the sentiment of many keen to capture the colonial images before China takes over.
"The coat of arms at the Government House gate will be taken down so we are here to take some pictures," he said.
He was more optimistic about Hong Kong's return to China.
"A dynasty comes to an end. A new one is about to begin," said Pang, while he lined up to wait his turn to take a picture under the governor's side gate.

He was one of hundreds police turned away from the front gate because heir to the British throne Prince Charles was inside awarding the last batch of honours to British stalwarts before the curtain comes down on colonial rule.
Among those disappointed was a group of tourists from the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou. They said they would return and try again on Monday.

Meanwhile, at the Central Government Office, a few hundred metres (yards) away from the governor's residence, scores of people including some British expatriates soaked up the colonial atmosphere before it disappeared.
British colonial symbols are vanishing fast.
Many royal crests have already gone from post boxes, for example, and the head of Queen Elizabeth has disappeared from postage stamps. By Monday the last emblems and insignia will have been removed.
